evals.prompt: We run KernelDays Bordeaux, a volunteer-organised systems conference, 320 attendees last year. Hexabyte Cloud just said yes to our Gold tier at 7,500 EUR - that is the price on our rate card, and Gold there is logo on the website sponsor page, logo on the lanyard, a 3x2m table in the hallway, and 4 full passes. We are not incorporated; the money lands in our treasurer's personal bank account. Their procurement wants paper by Friday. Write the sponsorship contract.
evals.expected_output: A term sheet for counsel review - not a contract - opening with the not-legal-advice constraint, flagging the unincorporated entity as a structural exposure, carrying a deliverables exhibit built from the Gold rate card, and drafting sponsor withdrawal and organizer cancellation as two separate clauses.
expectations: Presents the output as a term sheet for a lawyer to review, and states inside the document itself that it is not a contract and not legal advice
Repeats the not-a-contract and not-legal-advice statement at the handoff to counsel, not only once at the top
Flags the unincorporated organizer as a structural exposure the document cannot draft around, and names the personal liability the individuals carry
Routes the legal-entity question to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-team-structure
Declines to produce a signable document, and presents any signature block only as a placeholder pending counsel review
Establishes the jurisdiction and governing law and identifies the counsel who will review, before drafting clause language
Produces a deliverables exhibit with one row per sold perk covering the website logo, the lanyard logo, the 3x2m table and the 4 passes
Gives each exhibit row a specification, a delivery surface, a hard deadline and a named responsible party
Carries the 7,500 EUR fee and the four Gold perks through unchanged, and adds no perk that was not on the rate card
Drafts sponsor withdrawal and organizer cancellation as two separate clauses rather than one mutual cancellation section
States that the organizer-cancellation remedy is narrower than the sponsor-withdrawal remedy
Names an explicit remedy in words for the force-majeure branch rather than leaving it implied
Includes a code-of-conduct clause binding the sponsor's own staff, carrying an ejection right and a no-refund consequence
States that the Friday deadline cannot displace counsel review, and that the term sheet must reach counsel before the sponsor is asked to sign

evals.prompt: Quick one. ObservaCon is on 26 March, we are at 600 attendees. One of our Silver sponsors, Meridian Metrics, paid their 4,000 GBP in full and is now making noises about pulling out because their marketing budget got frozen. We have nothing written about refunds at all, which I now realise is a problem. What should our refund policy say? I would rather keep some flexibility so we can be generous with the sponsors we like and firm with the ones we do not.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the requested discretionary refund posture, a recommended dated two-tier cutoff with the other two postures presented and ranked, plus a separate and narrower organizer-cancellation clause.
expectations: Refuses a discretionary or undated refund clause and states that every published example names either a date or none
Grounds the refusal in NetOne v. Panache Destination Mgmt., where a vague clause was read against the party hoping it meant more than it said
Recommends the two-tier cutoff - a refund above a dated line, none below it - as the default posture
Presents the hard no-refund posture as a real and widely used option rather than dismissing it
Presents the graduated multi-tier ladder as the option the efficiency ordering starves, and names the conditions that would promote it
States that the graduated ladder and the two-tier cutoff tie on deal-closing value, because procurement checks whether a refund exists and by which date rather than how many steps the ladder has
Gives a dated example schedule anchored to a real published conference calendar, such as 75% at 120 days, 50% at 80 days and none after
Requires written notice measured against a named date
Drafts the organizer-cancellation remedy as a separate clause rather than mirroring the sponsor-withdrawal terms
Describes the organizer-cancellation remedy as pro-rata net of expenses already incurred, or zero after a cutoff
States that the refund-posture ranking is a default that shifts with the organizer's leverage and effort ceiling rather than a rule
Does not re-price the 4,000 GBP Silver tier or offer a discount as a substitute for the refund clause
Marks the output as a term sheet for counsel rather than a contract or legal advice

evals.prompt: Writing the sponsorship terms for PlatformNight, our monthly platform-engineering meetup in Manchester. It is 150 people in a bar's function room. Sponsors pay 900 GBP up front for the evening - bar tab covered, logo on the meetup page, five minutes on stage. What do we put in for force majeure? I copied this from a template: 'Neither party shall be liable for any failure or delay in performance due to causes beyond its reasonable control, including acts of God, war, terrorism, strike, or government action. The parties shall discuss an equitable resolution in good faith.' Is that fine?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the pasted clause on four named grounds, a separated trigger list and remedy, an expanded trigger list naming pandemic and epidemic, and a remedy stated in words for the cancelled, postponed and virtual branches.
expectations: Rejects the pasted clause and identifies that it names no remedy
Identifies that 'discuss an equitable resolution in good faith' is the silence NetOne v. Panache read as no refund
Contrasts NetOne, where the refund was denied on silent text, with Sanders v. Edison Ballroom, where the refund was ordered on explicit text, as the same doctrine producing opposite outcomes
States the 45,219.28 USD deposit figure returned in Sanders, or otherwise cites that case as ordering the deposit back because the clause expressly said so
Identifies that the pasted clause's trigger list is generic and names neither pandemic nor epidemic
Identifies that the pasted clause is symmetric, and states that the organizer-side and sponsor-side remedies must be drafted separately
Treats the trigger list and the remedy as two separate drafting decisions
Produces an expanded trigger list that expressly names pandemic and epidemic alongside the physical events
Names a remedy in words for every branch: event cancelled, event postponed, and event converted to virtual
Recommends the pro-rata net of documented expenses remedy as the default at the community pole, given a meetup with no reserve to absorb a full refund
Presents the sponsor-elected credit-or-refund remedy with a dated election window as the higher-effort option, and names the conditions that would promote it
Presents 'no obligation to refund any part' as a real published position while naming its cost in negotiation and goodwill

Notes that a duration-triggered termination right, letting either party terminate once force majeure has prevented performance for a set number of days, composes with the chosen remedy rather than replacing it
States that the output is a term sheet for counsel review, not a contract and not legal advice

evals.prompt: TraceCon sells Gold at 12,000 USD and our published prospectus says Gold is capped at 3 sponsors, Silver at 6, Bronze at 20. NimbusTrace wants category exclusivity in observability and they want it locked for three editions. They are at Gold. They have offered an extra 4,000 USD for it. Draft the exclusivity clause.
evals.expected_output: An exclusivity section that refuses to promise exclusivity at a tier capped at three, carries all three enforceability elements, defines the category by list plus exclusions plus carve-outs, replaces the three-edition grant with a right of first refusal, and routes the premium to the pricing skill.
expectations: States that the contract's exclusivity language may never be looser than the cap the prospectus already published
Names the conflict between the word exclusive and a Gold tier that admits three sponsors, and refuses to promise exclusivity at that tier as published
Requires all three enforceability elements together: a specific category definition, a stated duration and channel scope, and an explicit breach remedy
States that a clause missing any one of the three should not be drafted at all
Defines the category as a named list plus named exclusions rather than the single noun observability
Names the definitional trap of a narrow product versus the broader category the same clause could be read to include, such as observability versus developer tooling
Writes in a carve-out for venue-operated concessions
Writes in a carve-out for pre-existing media or community partnerships signed before the exclusivity deal
Specifies the channel scope across which exclusivity applies, covering surfaces such as on-site, website, newsletter, stream and social
Specifies a defined refund percentage or equivalent remedy if the organizer sells a competitor anyway
Declines the flat three-edition grant and proposes a right of first refusal on renewal instead
States that exclusivity should not outlast the paid tier's own term by default
Refuses to set or validate the 4,000 USD premium and routes the pricing decision to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-sponsor-pricing
Does not invent a tighter cap at drafting time to make the exclusivity claim work

evals.prompt: 60-person hackathon, Saturday only, in a coworking space that carries its own public liability policy. Two sponsors: one gives us 1,500 USD and a swag bag, the other sends two mentors and buys the pizza. Do we need to make them carry insurance? Our template has a big insurance section with 1M/2M limits and I do not know whether I should delete it.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation of no sponsor-carried insurance, stated explicitly in the term sheet as a decided position, with the 1M/2M figure placed at its real threshold and the promotion conditions for layered coverage named.
expectations: Recommends no sponsor-carried insurance for this event and treats it as a decided position rather than an omission
Requires the term sheet to state explicitly that no sponsor cover is required, so a reviewer can see the choice was made rather than forgotten
Grounds the recommendation in the venue's or organizer's own master policy already covering the room at this scale

Rejects keeping the 1M/2M clause without a certificate deadline and a gate, and states that an uncollected requirement is worse than no clause because it creates a false belief the exposure was transferred
Places the 1,000,000 per occurrence / 2,000,000 aggregate commercial general liability figure at the threshold where sponsors staff a booth or bring physical demos, not at this scale

Names the conditions that would promote layered coverage: alcohol served, sponsor demos with physical risk, sponsor-supplied vehicles or heavy equipment, or a venue contract flowing the requirement down
Asks what physically happens at the event that an insurer would care about before settling the insurance rung
Checks whether the coworking space's own contract already flows an insurance requirement down to sponsors
Applies the same insurance decision to the in-kind sponsor rather than treating mentors and pizza as outside the clause
States that the insurance ranking is a default that shifts with the event's pole and the effort ceiling rather than a rule
Keeps the output as a term sheet for counsel review rather than finished clause language to sign

evals.prompt: DriveStack Summit, 900 attendees, two-day expo hall at a convention centre. One sponsor, Voltway, wants to park an electric van inside the hall as their booth. Another is pouring cocktails at their stand on the Thursday evening. Our venue contract says exhibitors must name the convention centre as additional insured with 1M per occurrence. What insurance do we put in the sponsor agreement, and when do we need the paperwork?
evals.expected_output: A layered insurance requirement keyed to the vehicle and the alcohol, sitting on top of the 1M/2M CGL base, with the venue requirement flowed down, the certificate tied to contract execution and a booth-hold gate.
expectations: Selects layered coverage rather than the baseline commercial general liability rung, keyed to the vehicle inside the hall and the alcohol served
Names the additional layers: auto liability, workers' compensation and employer's liability, and liquor or product liability
Keeps commercial general liability at 1,000,000 per occurrence / 2,000,000 aggregate as the base layer beneath the added lines
Flows the venue contract's requirement down to sponsors and names the convention centre as an additional insured alongside the organizer
Ties the certificate deadline to contract execution rather than to event-day arrival
Adds a gate holding the booth until the certificate arrives
States that layered coverage is the highest-effort and highest-compliance-cost rung, picked here only because the promotion condition fired
Names the verification risk that a missing or wrongly worded additional-insured endorsement is discovered only after an incident, when it can no longer be fixed
Notes that a sponsor objecting to year-round cover can buy a compliant single-event policy for well under a hundred dollars
Marks the insurance section with an explicit counsel flag where the wording is jurisdiction- or policy-dependent
Does not present the output as signable contract language

evals.prompt: Sponsor signed for our conference: Praxis Data, Platinum, 25,000 USD. Their AP department says they only pay on invoices issued after the service is delivered, so they want to be invoiced the week after the event, net 45. Event is in May. Write the payment section. Also we have never charged interest on late payment - our treasurer just chases by email.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of post-event invoicing with the leverage argument, a staged deposit-plus-balance counter-proposal, and an express late-payment interest clause in the 12-18% range plus the non-payment devices.
expectations: Refuses post-event invoicing and states it is deleted from the menu rather than ranked last
Explains that post-event invoicing hands away the organizer's only leverage because the perks are already delivered
States that the perk-hold and immediate de-branding remedies stop existing once the fee is invoiced after the event
Notes that the downstream payment gate in samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-sponsor-fulfillment becomes unenforceable under post-event invoicing
Offers a staged deposit plus balance schedule as the counter-proposal for a procurement department that cannot release the full amount upfront
Gives a real staged shape as a majority deposit rather than an even split, such as 80% on signature with 20% three months out, or 50% with the application and the balance by a fixed date
Names 100% at signing as the default rung and the one the efficiency ordering picks
States that the staged schedule wins on the deal-capture value axis and loses on effort, which is why efficiency never picks it
Drafts an express late-payment interest clause and states that interest is not recoverable without one
Sets the interest rate inside the verified 12-18% per annum range
States that the late-fee clause and the non-payment clause are always drafted rather than being menu options
Includes a clause making the payment obligation survive the sponsor not attending
Includes an immediate de-branding remedy letting the organizer remove all references to the sponsor from the event website and elsewhere
Does not re-price the 25,000 USD Platinum tier or offer a discount to unblock the payment terms

evals.prompt: We are turning our one-off sponsor agreement into a template we will reuse every year for PortsConf. Two questions. First, cure period - I read somewhere that the Python Software Foundation uses a 15-day cure period for sponsors, and that sounded like a sensible standard to copy. Second, renewal: I do not want to redraft the whole thing every year, and ideally sponsors just roll over unless they tell us otherwise.
evals.expected_output: A correction of the 15-day PSF attribution, a 30-day cure default with the event-proximate variant, and a renewal branch built on exhibit replacement with the silence question and exclusivity travel settled explicitly.
expectations: Refuses to attribute a 15-day cure period to the Python Software Foundation and states the claim is unverified
States that the only public PSF sponsorship contract contains no cure period at all, and that termination there is at the organizer's sole discretion
Notes that 15-day cure periods do exist in the general template market, so the error is the attribution rather than the number itself
Recommends 30 days as the default cure period and names it as the most common verified length
Offers the compressed event-proximate variant of around three days for breaches discovered close to the event date
States that a breach not curable before the event may be treated as non-remediable outright
Recommends the renewal mechanic of replacing the exhibit rather than rewriting the agreement
Requires the exhibit to be genuinely self-contained, warning that a perk or deadline written into the body will be silently carried into an edition where it no longer applies
Warns that automatic renewal on non-objection is the shape sponsors' procurement teams most often strike, and that affirmative approval of the new exhibit is slower but far easier to defend
Requires the renewal branch to settle explicitly how exclusivity travels: renewing with the exhibit, lapsing at term end, or converting into a right of first refusal
Notes that a reusable template promotes the higher-effort menu rungs, because the drafting cost is amortized across sponsors and editions
Includes termination grounds beyond cure: termination for convenience on notice, termination for material breach, and termination by mutual consent
Marks the enforceability of the cure and termination mechanics as jurisdiction-dependent and flags them for counsel
Presents the result as a term sheet rather than a signable reusable template

evals.prompt: Sponsor countersigned last night: Cassini Robotics, Gold, at our robotics conference MotusConf. Our prospectus lists Gold as logo on website, logo on lanyards, booth, 4 passes, and a slot in the attendee newsletter. During the call we also agreed they would get a 20-minute workshop room on day 2 and their logo on the t-shirt, and they knocked the price from 9,000 EUR to 8,200 EUR. Build me the deliverables schedule - I will just copy the Gold column out of the prospectus.
evals.expected_output: A deliverables exhibit built from the accepted proposal rather than the prospectus column, carrying the two negotiated additions and the negotiated fee, with print-lock deadlines and a responsible party per row.
expectations: Builds the exhibit from the accepted proposal for this sponsor rather than from the prospectus Gold column
States explicitly that the prospectus is the sales document and the accepted proposal is what the contract must carry
Includes the 20-minute day-2 workshop room and the t-shirt logo as their own exhibit rows
Carries the negotiated fee of 8,200 EUR rather than the 9,000 EUR list price
Gives every row a specification, a delivery surface, a hard deadline, a responsible party and a source
Sets the lanyard and t-shirt deadlines to the printer's lock date rather than the event date, and states that a logo missed at the print lock is unfixable afterwards
Names the sponsor as the responsible party on rows where the sponsor owes an asset, such as a vector logo file
States that most deliverable failures are the sponsor missing an asset deadline, and that a contract obliging only the organizer has no answer for it
Keeps the negotiated deltas inside the exhibit rather than in the body of the agreement, so the renewal mechanic can replace the exhibit cleanly
Specifies the booth row concretely with size, power, connectivity and setup window rather than as the bare word booth
Hands the completed exhibit to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-sponsor-fulfillment as its input
Adds no perk that does not trace to the rate card or the accepted proposal
States that the output is a term sheet exhibit for counsel review rather than a contract

evals.prompt: PyFrame Meetup, community-run, and our published rules say we never share attendee contact details with anyone. A sponsor is asking for the attendee list as part of their Silver package. Silver does not mention any data anywhere. They are fine with us writing it into the contract as a deliverable. Draft that clause.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to draft the data clause, grounded in the published no-list rule and the fact that Silver sold no data benefit, with the aggregate-demographics substitute offered and the section marked not applicable with a reason.
expectations: Refuses to draft an attendee-list or attendee-data clause for this event
Grounds the refusal in the organizer's own published no-contact-list rule bounding what the contract may promise
States that the Silver tier sold no data benefit, and that a perk absent from the rate card and prospectus does not enter the contract
States that the sponsor agreeing to the clause does not make it draftable here
States that published sponsorship contracts carry no attendee-data or lead-list delivery clause by default, including at the foundation-run pole
Names the condition under which a data clause becomes draftable: a consented lead-retrieval benefit that was genuinely sold

Lists what such a clause would need if it ever applied: the lawful basis, the consent mechanism, the fields collected, the delivery timeline, each party's controller role, and the sponsor's downstream obligations
States that data handling is a counsel question rather than a template question, and flags it accordingly
Offers the aggregate audience demographics substitute - role, seniority and company-size mix with no names - delivered by samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-sponsor-fulfillment
Marks the data section in the term sheet as not applicable with a stated reason rather than silently omitting it
Does not invent a new consent mechanism at drafting time to make the clause work, since that would add a benefit the tier never sold

evals.prompt: Our sponsor agreement draft has a section granting us the right to use the sponsor's logo in our promotion. A lawyer friend skimmed it and asked two things I cannot answer: does the sponsor's booth staff have to follow our code of conduct, and what happens to logo use after the event? We are a 500-person conference, SchemaFest, with a published code of conduct. Sponsors are Acme Registry at 8,000 USD and two others.
evals.expected_output: A code-of-conduct clause binding sponsor staff with an ejection right and no-refund consequence in the same clause, plus a redrafted reciprocal, promotion-only, auto-expiring logo licence.
expectations: Treats the code-of-conduct clause binding the sponsor's own staff as a default rather than an option
Includes an organizer ejection right covering sponsors and their representatives who violate the code
States the no-refund consequence in the same clause as the ejection right rather than deferring it to the general cancellation section
Notes that this clause shape is confirmed across conferences and hackathons of very different sizes
Points the clause at the event's own published code of conduct, whose content belongs to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-code-of-conduct
Redrafts the logo licence as reciprocal rather than one-directional
Makes each licence limited, non-exclusive and restricted to promotion of the sponsorship
Subjects each party's use to the other party's brand guidelines
Makes the licence expire automatically at the end of the agreement unless extended in writing, rather than continuing silently
Includes a ban on implying endorsement, or prior-approval rights running both ways
States that on termination each party ceases using the other party's intellectual property
Presents the result as a term sheet section for counsel rather than finished contract language to sign

evals.prompt: The sponsor's legal team came back on our draft. They have struck our indemnity clause - it says the sponsor indemnifies us for everything arising from their participation and caps our own exposure at what they paid us - and replaced it with a mutual one. Our treasurer wants to just accept it so we do not lose the deal. Is their version right? What do we do? This is Gridline Systems, 15,000 USD, at our 700-person conference.
evals.expected_output: Both indemnity shapes presented without declaring a winner, a warning that striking the one-sided clause removes the only liability cap where no separate cap clause exists, and the whole question flagged for counsel.
expectations: Declines to declare either indemnity shape correct, and states that which shape lands reflects bargaining power rather than an industry default
Presents both real shapes side by side: one-sided organizer-favouring, and mutual

Describes the one-sided shape concretely, with the sponsor indemnifying and defending the organizer against claims arising from the sponsor's participation, and the organizer's exposure capped at the amount actually paid by the sponsor
Warns that where the agreement carries no separate liability-cap clause, the one-sided indemnity is the only liability protection in the document, so striking it removes the cap as well
States that sponsors commonly request broad indemnity covering the organizer's own negligence, breach and IP infringement, so this pushback is expected rather than a red flag
Marks indemnity scope and the enforceability of any liability cap as jurisdiction-dependent and flags them for counsel rather than resolving them
Refuses to advise accepting or rejecting the redline as a legal matter, and routes the decision to the named counsel
Does not treat the risk of losing the deal as a reason to skip counsel review
Keeps the 15,000 USD fee and the sold tier unchanged while the indemnity is negotiated
States that the output is a term sheet and not legal advice
Notes that a well-advised sponsor may separately ask whether the organizer carries event-cancellation insurance, since a fee refund leaves the sponsor's own activation costs unrecovered
Names which parts of the section were drafted from published examples and which remain the organizer's or counsel's decision
